items.basis: Radiative cooling coatings require clear sky conditions to effectively reject heat to the cold of space, which is not guaranteed in the variable cloud conditions typical of vaccine transport routes, rendering the mechanism unreliable for maintaining consistent cooling

The proposed solution ignores the critical boundary condition of salt-clogged wicks, which would prevent evaporative cooling from functioning at all, making the radiative coating alone insufficient to maintain the required 8°C temperature threshold

The cited evidence [doi:10.1016/j.renene.2023.04.141] studies radiative cooling on chemical storage tanks, not vaccine coolers, and addresses evaporative loss control, not temperature maintenance, making it irrelevant to the specific vaccine cooling problem

The claimed 48-hour cooling duration at 40°C ambient with high humidity and salt-clogged wick is not supported by any evidence and contradicts known physics of passive cooling systems, which typically fail under such conditions

The coating would require precise application to maintain emissivity properties in the atmospheric transparency window, which is impossible to achieve consistently on the curved, irregular surfaces of evaporative coolers in last-mile clinic settings

The testable prediction compares coated vs uncooled coolers, but fails to establish baseline performance metrics for the uncooled version under identical high-humidity conditions with salt-clogged wicks, making the comparison meaningless
